item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 15:00

Josef Průša is a Czech inventor. He changes the world of 3D printing.

As a student, he likes working with music equipment. He needs special parts for his projects. So, he decides to build his own 3D printer. His design becomes very popular. In 2012, he starts a company called Prusa Research in Prague. Today, the company sells printers all over the world and works with big organizations like NASA and Mercedes. Many small businesses also use his printers to make creative products.

Josef Průša believes that 3D printing can help more people create and build new things in Europe and beyond.

Difficult words: inventor (a person who creates something new), creative (able to make or think of new interesting ideas), beyond (further than).

item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 15:00

Josef Průša is a Czech entrepreneur and engineer who became one of Europe’s most influential people in 3D printing. As a student, he experimented with music technology and built his first 3D printer to make customized parts.

His design quickly gained global interest, and in 2012, he founded Prusa Research in Prague. The company now employs over 1,000 people and sells 3D printers to customers on every continent, including large organizations such as NASA, Mercedes, and MIT.

Průša’s open-source approach inspires countless small companies to innovate using cheaper printers locally. He believes 3D printing can bring manufacturing back to Europe by helping entrepreneurs design, produce, and compete independently.

Difficult words: entrepreneur (someone who starts and manages their own business), influential (having the power to change people’s opinions or the way things develop), customized (made or changed to fit one person’s or company’s special needs), open-source approach (a way of working where people share their software or designs freely so others can use, change, and improve them).

item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 15:00

Czech visionary Josef Průša has redefined additive manufacturing through his pioneering 3D printing technology.

Originally a student fascinated by music equipment, he engineered his own self-replicating 3D printer, an innovation that soon became an industry standard.

In 2012, he left university to establish Prusa Research, which has since evolved into a global enterprise based in Prague. The firm employs more than 1,200 people, exports worldwide, and generates annual revenues exceeding 160 million euros. Its award-winning machines are used by leading institutions such as NASA, CERN, and MIT, as well as numerous startups.

Průša’s philosophy centers on decentralizing production and stimulating European innovation. By making high-quality 3D printing accessible, he envisions a future where creativity, technology, and sustainability merge to reshape manufacturing across the continent.

Difficult words: visionary (a person with original ideas about what the future could be like), decentralize (to spread control or production away from one main place to several smaller ones), merge (to join two or more things together to become one).

item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 07:00

England will let local leaders add a small tax to overnight hotel stays. People who stay in hotels, B&Bs, or holiday homes will pay a little extra money, usually under 5% of the room cost.

Some cities like Manchester already have a tax of 1 pound (1.14 euros) per room. The new plan will start before 2029. Many hotel owners do not like this new tax. They worry that visitors will go to other places to save money.

Studies show that a 10-pound (11.40 euros) fee might make people visit less. But each local leader can choose to use the tax or say no to it.

Difficult words: add (to put something together with something else), tax (money that people must pay to the government to pay for public services), fee (money which you pay for a particular service).

item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 07:00

England will soon allow local mayors to charge a tourist tax on overnight hotel stays.

The tax will cover all types of places to stay, like hotels, B&Bs, and holiday homes. Mayors can choose the exact price, but most plan to keep it under 5% of the total room bill.

Cities like Manchester, which charges 1 pound (1.14 euros) per room, and Edinburgh already use similar fees. The new tax will likely start before 2029. Many businesses in the tourism industry are unhappy about the new tax. They worry that visitors will choose other places to travel to avoid paying extra fees, which could lead to a 1.8 billion pound (2.1 billion euros) loss in tourism spending. Studies show that many tourists might stay fewer nights or spend less money.

Mayors don’t have to introduce the tax, and some local leaders already said no to the plan.

Difficult words: mayor (an elected leader of a city or town government), likely (expected to happen or very probable), avoid (to stay away from a person, place, or situation).

You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

item.content:encoded:
16-09-2026 07:00

The UK government will allow mayors in England to introduce a tourist tax on overnight stays before 2029. The levy will apply to all accommodation types, including hotels, B&Bs, and short-term rentals, regardless of the visitor’s nationality or purpose.

While the charge is uncapped, local leaders, including London’s mayor, expect to keep it under 5% of the total accommodation cost. Similar fees are already operational in Manchester and Edinburgh, following widespread adoption across continental Europe. However, the hospitality sector has strongly criticized the decision. Experts warn that a 5% tax could reduce tourism spending by 1.8 billion pounds (2.1 billion euros) and destroy nearly 33,000 jobs by 2030. Furthermore, extra fees might deter both international and domestic travelers and drive them toward destinations without visitor levies.

Difficult words: levy (an official amount of money, such as a tax, that a government or organization collects), operational (ready to use, working, or actively in service), hospitality sector (businesses that provide services like hotels, restaurants, bars, and travel).

Gamescom is the world’s biggest event for video games. More than 350,000 people visit to play new games.

This time, the event shows big news, like a new remake of The Witcher 3. Xbox celebrates 25 years and wants to make games cheaper for everyone. Famous characters like Lara Croft from Tomb Raider are coming back with new graphics. Small teams of workers are also making big games today. The company Nvidia shows new AI tools. They make games look like real life. Gamescom is a fun place for people to meet and play together.

Difficult words: remake (a new version of an older game, movie, or song), character (a person, animal, or creature in a story, movie, or video game), graphics (the visual images, colors, and designs on a screen).

item.content:encoded:
15-09-2026 15:00

Gamescom is the world’s biggest gaming event, with over 350,000 visitors. The event started with big news, including a new version of The Witcher 3.

At the show, Xbox celebrated its 25th birthday, and its new leader said the gaming industry needs to make hardware more affordable. Classic games are also coming back; Tomb Raider is getting a modern update called Legacy of Atlantis with better graphics and controls. Smaller game studios are working on big projects too. A small team from Scotland is making a new horror game called Silent Hill Townfall. Furthermore, technology companies like Nvidia showed new AI tools to make game graphics look very real in real time.

Gamescom remains an exciting place where fans and developers meet to play new games.

Difficult words: affordable (cheap enough for most people to be able to buy or pay for), update (a change which makes something more modern or accurate), remain (to continue to be in the same state, condition, or place).

item.content:encoded:
15-09-2026 15:00

Gamescom, the world’s largest in-person gaming convention, opened with Opening Night Live and featured major announcements like a remake of The Witcher 3.

Over 350,000 visitors are expected at the massive event that fills ten halls with major publishers and indie developers.

CEO Asha Sharma marked Xbox’s 25th anniversary and emphasized that the industry must innovate on efficiency and hardware affordability. Classic franchises are also making headlines; Tomb Raider is being reimagined as Legacy of Atlantis with modernized gameplay while it honors Lara Croft’s iconic confidence.

Smaller independent studios are stepping up to handle huge intellectual properties. Scottish team Screenburn is developing Silent Hill Townfall. Tech advancements are equally prominent – Nvidia demonstrates DLSS 5, a generative AI graphics tool that renders hyper-realistic visuals in real time. Gamescom highlights how the industry is adapting to new challenges, balancing iconic remakes with groundbreaking technology to shape gaming’s future.

Difficult words: convention (a large meeting where people with similar interests or jobs gather together), indie (made by a small, independent company without backing from a big corporation), render (to create a final visual image or video on a computer screen using specialized software).

item.content:encoded:
15-09-2026 07:00

In Gambia, many people do not have electricity. Some places have no power for two days in the hot weather.

People are very angry because their food spoils. Shops cannot work. Protesters walk in the streets. They make fires and block roads. Police use tear gas to stop them. President Adama Barrow calls the problem a big emergency. He says that the government will bring a new power machine by the end of October 2026.

Officials say that hot weather causes the troubles. This is a big problem because the country has an election in December.

Difficult words: spoil (to go bad), tear gas (gas which police use to control angry people), trouble (a problem).

You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
